gist: Atwood opens the exoteric part of the book by setting aside questions of alchemy's temporal origin and name in favour of its means and principles, introduces Hermes Trismegistus and his writings (distinguishing the theosophic books from the Golden Treatise, which gives the physical ground and practical method), quotes the Smaragdine Table as the compressed principle and subject of the art, and presents Egypt's fall, with the Asclepian prophecy, as the loss of a superior sacred science through abuse and over-exposure.

notes.point: Part I is an 'Exoteric View' of alchemy; Chapter I surveys Hermetic philosophy's public history.

The Hermetic tradition opens early in the East, its monuments and records dark and enigmatical. Its origin (variously Adam, Noah, Cham, Solomon, Zoroaster, Hermes) is set aside: the inquiry concerns means and principles of occult science; eternal truth does not always originate where it is understood.

She leaves open the Syriadic pillars, Egypt or Palestine, and the Smaragdine table's authorship; alchemy is antique, perhaps coeval with the universe. Against Conringius's 'recent invention', Kircher, Borrichius, Vallensis and Greek authors suffice, though Egyptian record has perished.
A brief history of alchemical philosophers will show her later propositions are not gratuitous; English histories of philosophy neglect this once influential branch.

Per Plutarch, Egypt was called Cham or Chemia for its black soil; others derive name and art from Cham, who first practised the art of Vulcan there. Chemia also meant the eye's pupil and black matters, perhaps why alchemy was called a Black Art.

Etymology corroborates but cannot discover. She begins with Hermes Trismegistus, adept king (per Suidas c. 400 years before Moses), famed for skill in nature's secret operations and the 'quintessential perfectibility of the three kingdoms'; hence 'Thrice Great'.

His books perished under Dioclesian; the Asclepian Dialogues and Poimander survive (Ficinus; Everard). The Poimander could move a skeptic to intelligible reality. These books treat divine capabilities and regeneration, not their physical ground, which with the practical method is in the Tractatus Aureus. The Smaragdine Table is said to contain the art's working principle and total subject.

Table: above as below, for the miracles of the One Thing, from which all arose by adaptation; Sun father, Moon mother, wind carrier, Earth nurse; power integral if turned into earth; separate earth from fire, subtle from gross, gently; it ascends, descends, gains strength of superiors and inferiors; overcomes subtle, penetrates solid; so the world was created; it concerns the operation of the Sun.

The Table is all that remains of Egypt's Sacred Art. Her ruins evidence lost, superior science; Pythagoras, Thales, Democritus and Plato were initiated there into that Art, by which Egypt governed, keeping the profane in abeyance, until self-abuse and neglect of her law brought ruin, as foretold.

Asclepian prophecy: religion becomes fables, divinity returns to heaven, darkness preferred, the religious counted insane, death for followers of the 'Religion of Intellect', divine voice silenced, earth and air corrupted.

Atwood rejects the modern charge of forgery: the prophecy foretold a falling off, but early Christianity was a revival; Lactantius and Augustine cite it without doubt. Faith then rested on 'reality and living operation'; regeneration was rationally understood. Egypt's fulfilment came partly later, when sacred mysteries over-exposed to the multitude were perverted.

method.veiled: an inquiry which rather relates to the means and principles of occult science than to the period and place of their reputed discovery
method.plain: The book's concern is how the occult science works and on what principles, not its history of origin.

also.text: observe not how truth, being everywhere eternal, does not there always originate where it is understood

method.veiled: words do not convey true ideas unless their proper leader be previously entertained
method.plain: Words reveal their real meaning only to someone who already holds the guiding idea; word-study can confirm a truth once suggested but cannot discover it.

also.text: Etymological research has doubtless proved useful in leading on and corroborating truths once suggested, but it is not a way of first discovery

method.veiled: denote rather our divine capabilities and promise of regeneration than the physical ground of either
method.plain: The Poimander and Asclepian books describe human divine capacities and the promise of regeneration, not their physical ground; that physical ground, together with alchemy's practical method, is said to be given in the Golden Treatise.

also.text: this, with the practical method of alchemy being further given in the Tractatus Aureus, or Golden Treatise

method.veiled: is said to comprehend the working principle and total subject of the art
method.plain: The Smaragdine Table is said to state, in a few lines, both the operative principle and the whole subject-matter of alchemy.

method.veiled: the quintessential perfectibility of the three kingdoms in their homogeneal unity
method.plain: Hermes' reputed discovery: three 'kingdoms' share one homogeneous nature and can be perfected to a quintessence. This chunk does not name the three kingdoms.
method.basis: I.1 ¶6, read literally; the parallel 'having the Three Parts of the philosophy of the whole world' (I.1 ¶9) and 'all things arose from this one thing' (I.1 ¶9) support a single common nature, but neither identifies the kingdoms.

method.veiled: whence he is called the Thrice Great Hermes, having the spiritual intelligence of all things in their universal law
method.plain: Hermes is called 'Thrice Great' because of his reputed discovery about the three kingdoms: he had spiritual understanding of all things under their universal law.

also.text: Therefore I am I called Thrice Great Hermes, having the Three Parts of the philosophy of the whole world

method.veiled: that which is above is as that which is below, and that which is below is as that which is above, for performing the miracles of the One Thing
method.plain: Higher and lower correspond; this correspondence is what makes the work on the One Thing possible.
method.basis: I.1 ¶9: the clause 'for performing the miracles of the One Thing' ties the correspondence to the work; the chunk gives no further gloss.

method.plain: The single subject of the work, from which all things arose by adaptation and which is called the father of all perfection. This chunk does not say what it is.
method.basis: I.1 ¶9 'all things arose from this one thing by adaptation', 'This is the father of all perfection'; I.1 ¶7 says the Table comprehends the 'total subject of the art'.

also.text: as all things were from one, by the mediation of one, so all things arose from this one thing by adaptation

method.veiled: So the world was created. Hence were all wonderful adaptations of which this is the manner.
method.plain: The process described for the One Thing is the same process by which the world was created; the work follows the pattern of creation.
method.basis: I.1 ¶9: 'So the world was created' follows directly on the description of the operation; 'as all things were from one ... so all things arose from this one thing'.

method.veiled: the father of it is the Sun, the mother of it is the Moon; the wind carries it in its belly; the nurse thereof is the Earth
method.plain: The One Thing is generated from two principles called Sun and Moon, carried by 'wind' and nourished by 'Earth'. This chunk does not explain these names.
method.basis: I.1 ¶9 only; the parentage imagery is given without gloss.

method.veiled: The power of it is Integral, if it be turned into earth.
method.plain: The One Thing's power becomes integral (complete) when it is turned into earth. Not explained in this chunk.
method.basis: I.1 ¶9, literal reading; 'it ascends from earth to heaven, and again descends to earth' in the same paragraph also ends in earth.

method.veiled: Thou shalt separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the gross, gently with much sagacity
method.plain: A separation of earth from fire and of subtle from gross, done gently and with great judgment. This chunk does not say which part corresponds to which.
method.basis: I.1 ¶9: the two clauses are set in apposition; 'gently with much sagacity' gives the manner. Pairing of the terms is open (see ambiguities).

method.veiled: it ascends from earth to heaven, and again descends to earth: and receives the strength of the superiors and of the inferiors
method.plain: After separation the subject rises and falls again, a circulation through which it gathers the powers of both higher and lower; this is when it attains 'the glory of the whole world'. Not further explained here.
method.basis: I.1 ¶9: sequence follows the separation instruction and is followed by 'so thou hast the glory of the whole world'; links to 'that which is above is as that which is below'.

method.veiled: This is the strong fortitude of all fortitudes, overcoming every subtle and penetrating every solid thing.
method.plain: The completed product is the strongest power, prevailing over both subtle and solid things. Not explained in this chunk.

also.text: so thou hast the glory of the whole world; therefore let all obscurity flee before thee
This is the father of all perfection, or consummation of the whole world.

method.veiled: For what else, but for the knowledge of that mighty Art with which she arose, governed, and dazzled the whole contemporary world
method.plain: The wisdom into which Egypt initiated Greek philosophers was the alchemical Art itself; it was also the basis of Egypt's government and power.
method.basis: I.1 ¶10: rhetorical questions linking initiation of Pythagoras, Thales, Democritus, Plato to 'that mighty Art'; I.1 ¶10 calls the Table what remains of Egypt's 'Sacred Art'.

method.veiled: sacred mysteries, too openly exposed to the multitude, became perverted and vilified by their abuse
method.plain: Sacred knowledge is corrupted when exposed too openly to the multitude and when its law is neglected; Egypt preserved her Art by keeping the profane in abeyance.
method.basis: I.1 ¶11 states the over-exposure of 'sacred mysteries'; I.1 ¶10 ties Egypt's fall to self-abuse and neglect of 'the law, by which she governed' while she held the profane in abeyance. Equating the 'sacred mysteries' with the Art itself is inference.

also.text: holding in strong abeyance the ignorant, profane, vulgar, until the evil day of desolation came with self-abuse, when, neglecting to obey the law, by which she governed, all fell

method.veiled: faith was then grounded in reality and living operation, and the mystery of human regeneration, so zealously proclaimed, was also rationally understood
method.plain: Atwood holds that human regeneration was once understood rationally, as a real, living operation and not merely a belief.

also.text: the Spirit of the Word was potent in faith to heal and save
